questions.prompt: What does this jagged array code print?
options: It throws an `IndexOutOfRangeException`, because row 0 has only 2 elements
questions.explanation: Each row of a jagged array is a separate array and rows can have different lengths. `jagged[1]` is `{ 3, 4, 5 }`, and index 2 of it is 5.
`Length` is the total number of elements in all dimensions, so a 2 × 2 array has length 4. The number of dimensions is `Rank`, which is 2 here.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares a rectangular (multi-dimensional) array with a jagged array?
options: A rectangular array lets rows have different lengths; a jagged array does not
A jagged array is stored in one continuous block; a rectangular array stores each row separately
A rectangular array is one continuous block with equal-length rows; a jagged array stores each row as a separate object, so rows can differ in length
Both are stored the same way and differ only in syntax
questions.explanation: A rectangular array is stored in a single continuous block with all rows the same length (cache-friendly). In a jagged array each row is a separate object, so rows can vary, at the cost of extra memory references.

questions.prompt: Why does the note recommend `List<T>` over `ArrayList` in modern code?
options: `ArrayList` stores elements as `object`, so value types are boxed and there is no type safety
`ArrayList` cannot grow after it is created
questions.explanation: `ArrayList` is a non-generic legacy class that stores elements as `object`, so boxing/unboxing occurs for value types. `List<T>` is generic, type-safe, avoids boxing and performs better.

options: Removes three elements starting at index 1 and shrinks the array
Sets three elements, starting at index 1, to the default value
Deletes the elements at indexes 1 and 3
Clears the whole array and resizes it to 3 elements
questions.explanation: `Clear(array, startIndex, length)` sets a range of elements to the default value. Arrays have a fixed size, so nothing is removed.
